column4: Behind every ticker on your screen is a real business, with real products, real customers, and real revenue. Fundamental analysis asks one plain question. Is this actually a good company, and is it priced fairly? In this lesson you will learn to read a company the way an owner would, using its financial statements and a few key numbers. Let's look behind the ticker.

There are two very different ways to size up a stock. Technical analysis reads the chart, the price, the patterns, the story of what buyers and sellers are doing right now. Fundamental analysis reads the company itself, its financial statements, its industry, and the wider economy, to estimate what the business is really worth and how fast it can grow. On screen you can see the split, chart on one side, company on the other. They answer different questions, and strong investors learn to use both.

Every public company reports its health through three financial statements. The income statement shows revenue, expenses, and net income over a period, so it tells you whether the company actually made money. The balance sheet is a snapshot at a single point in time, assets on one side, liabilities and equity on the other, so it tells you what the company owns and what it owes. The cash flow statement tracks real cash moving through the business, split into operating, investing, and financing activities. Look at the three cards on screen. Together they give you the full picture.

column3: P E, E P S and Health
column4: Now the numbers investors watch most. Earnings per share, or E P S, is the company's profit divided across its shares, the slice of profit attributed to each share you own. The price to earnings ratio, P E, takes the share price and divides it by E P S. It tells you how much the market is paying for each dollar of earnings, and it only means something when you compare it to similar companies. Two more health checks. The current ratio measures short term liquidity, whether the company can cover its near term bills. Debt to equity measures leverage, how much it borrows against what owners have put in. And remember, stocks move on catalysts, earnings reports and major news. Companies file a ten K each year, a ten Q each quarter, and an eight K for major events.

Your turn. On screen is a simple P E calculator. Type in a share price and the earnings per share, and it works out the price to earnings ratio for you. Try a few combinations and watch the big number change. A lower P E can mean the stock is cheaper, or that the market expects slower growth. A higher P E can mean pricier, or faster expected growth. The number alone never tells you enough, so always compare it to peers. And if earnings are zero or negative, the ratio simply is not meaningful. These figures are illustrative examples, not advice.

Let's practice spotting a healthy business from a shaky one. Sort the cards yourself. Each one describes something you might find in a company's numbers. Decide whether it points to strength or is a warning sign, then drop it in the right column. Growing earnings and manageable debt point to strength. Losing money quarter after quarter and costs outrunning revenue are red flags. Work through all eight and lock in the pattern.
Five quick questions to lock it all in. Answer each one to earn your points for the lesson.

Let's carry the essentials with you. Fundamental analysis reads the company, technical analysis reads the chart. The three statements are the income statement, the balance sheet, and the cash flow statement. E P S is profit per share, and P E shows what the market pays for each dollar of earnings, best judged against peers. Catalysts like earnings and major news move stocks.
